lessons.title: Interest and aptitude questionnaire
lessons.body:
There are no right answers here. Answer honestly and quickly; your first instinct is usually the true one.

This questionnaire feeds into your Stream Recommendation Report at the end of week 2, together with how the four taster lessons go.

questions.q: When something breaks at home (a fan, a tap, the wifi), what do you usually do?
options: Try to open it and figure out why
Look up how it works and who to call
Think about what it costs to fix vs replace

questions.q: Which of these would you read for fun?
options: How vaccines train the immune system
How a company went from a garage to a billion dollars

questions.q: A long maths problem that takes 20 minutes feels...
options: Fine if I see the point

questions.q: In a group project you naturally...
options: Plan, budget and keep people on track

questions.q: Pick the sentence closest to you
options: I like knowing exactly why something is true
I like living things and how bodies work
I like money, markets and how businesses run
I like people, stories and arguments

lessons.title: Why does double the speed give four times the height?
lessons.body:
1 · Hook

A cricketer throws a ball straight up at 15 m/s. It reaches about 11 metres. Her friend throws at 30 m/s, exactly double. How high does his go? Most people say 22 m. The real answer is 45 m. Not double. Four times.

Why? Don't read ahead. Find out below by throwing balls yourself.

2 · Play

Pick a speed, type your guess for the height first, then throw. Do it at least three times with very different speeds. Wrong guesses are the whole point; that's how your brain notices the pattern.

[[widget:ball-throw]]

3 · Name it

What you just found has a name. When something is thrown straight up with speed u and gravity pulls it down at g (about 10 m/s² on Earth):

height = u² ÷ (2g) and time in the air = 2u ÷ g

Check it against your table: 20 m/s gives 400 ÷ 20 = 20 m and 4 s. The u² is why doubling the speed quadruples the height. That's the only new thing in Class 11 kinematics: in Class 10 you plugged into formulas; in Class 11 you're expected to know why the formula has that shape. You now do.

Where it comes from, if you're curious: at the top the ball's speed is zero. Using v² = u² + 2as with v = 0 and a = −g gives s = u²/2g. Same equation you had in Class 10, just used with a sign.

4 · Do it

Four questions below. Use the hints. Every one is a thing you just saw happen.

5 · AI twist

Open ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude and ask: "If I throw a ball up at 30 m/s, how high does it go? Explain like I'm 15."

Now check it against your table and the formula. Did it get 45 m? Did it explain the square? Did it say anything you can prove wrong with your own throws? Write one line about it in your diary at the end of this week. This is the real skill: using AI and knowing when you're the one who's right.

questions.q: You throw at 10 m/s. Your friend throws at 20 m/s. His ball goes how many times higher than yours?
questions.hint: Look at your table. Height goes with the square of the speed.
questions.explain: Height ∝ u². Double the speed, 4× the height: 5 m vs 20 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown straight up at 30 m/s (g = 10). Maximum height?
questions.explain: 900 ÷ 20 = 45 m. That's the cricketer's friend from the hook.

questions.q: Same stone. How long until it's back in the hand?
questions.hint: Time in the air = 2u ÷ g. Up and down take equal time.

questions.q: At the very top of its flight, the ball's velocity and acceleration are...
questions.hint: Watch the sim: the ball stops for an instant, but gravity never switches off.
questions.explain: Velocity is momentarily zero; acceleration stays 10 m/s² downward the whole time. That's why it comes back down.

questions.q: Honest check: this lesson felt mostly like...
options: Interesting, I'd do more of this

lessons.title: What an AI model actually is
lessons.body:
Everything you will use this summer, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, is a language model. Here is the whole idea in four steps.

  1. Text becomes numbers. Words are chopped into tokens, roughly chunks of words, and each token becomes a list of numbers.
  2. The model predicts the next token. That is all it does. Given everything so far, it guesses what comes next, then does it again, and again.
  3. It learned by reading. It was trained on a huge amount of text and adjusted billions of internal numbers until its guesses got good.
  4. It does not look things up. Unless connected to a tool, it has no database. It produces the most likely continuation. That is why it can be fluent and wrong at the same time. This is called a hallucination.

Watch

In the video, a model runs on an ordinary PC in the mentor's room. Watch it generate one token at a time. There is no magic box; it is a program.

What this means for you

Treat the model like a very well-read friend who never admits when they are unsure. Brilliant for explaining, drafting and practising. Dangerous for facts you have not checked.

questions.q: What does a language model fundamentally do?
options: Predicts the next token given the text so far
Stores every fact in a database
questions.explain: It predicts the next token, repeatedly. Everything else is built on that.

questions.q: Why can a model state something false with total confidence?
options: It produces likely-sounding text, not verified facts
It was trained only on fiction
questions.hint: Fluent is not the same as true.
questions.explain: It generates the most probable continuation, which can be wrong. Always verify facts.

options: A chunk of a word or a short word
questions.explain: Tokens are word pieces; 'unbelievable' might be 3 tokens.

lessons.title: Your AI-use diary: the first experiment
lessons.body:
This week's build task is small on purpose. Open any AI chat (ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, free versions are fine) and do these three things. Write what happened in your diary below.

  1. Ask it to explain the kinematics problem from the PCM taster in a different way than the lesson did. Was it clearer? Was anything wrong?
  2. Ask it something you already know the answer to from Class 10. Did it get it right?
  3. Ask it for a fact about your own town or school. Check it. Was it correct?

Submit your diary as this week's checkpoint by Friday. Three honest paragraphs is enough.

questions.q: A body starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Final velocity?
A train slows from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over 100 m. Deceleration?
The slope of a velocity–time graph gives...
questions.explain: Slope of v–t is acceleration; area under it is displacement.
